title: NumPy
description: Check that you can express calculations over whole arrays instead of looping.

lessons.title: Creating and describing arrays
lessons.lead: An ndarray is a grid of one type, with a shape. Everything else in NumPy follows from that.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `[1, 2] * 2` and `np.array([1, 2]) * 2`?
options: The list repeats to `[1, 2, 1, 2]`; the array doubles each element to `[2, 4]`
The array version raises a TypeError
questions.explain: Operators on an array are element-wise. This is the single biggest behavioural difference from a list.
Like `range`, the stop value is excluded. `np.linspace(0, 10, 5)` is the version that does include the endpoint.

questions.prompt: Which attributes describe a NumPy array?
options: `.dtype`  the single type of every element
questions.explain: There is no `.length`. The element count is `.size`, and `len()` gives the first dimension only.
`argmax` returns the position of the largest value, not the value itself  useful for looking up the matching name in a parallel array.

lessons.title: Masks, slices, and views
lessons.lead: How you select data  and NumPy's biggest surprise about what you get back.

questions.explain: The comparison builds a boolean mask; indexing with that mask keeps only the positions where it is True.

questions.prompt: Why must you write `scores[(scores > 50) & (scores < 90)]` rather than using `and`?
options: `and` cannot work element-wise and raises a ValueError
`&` is the only operator NumPy defines
questions.explain: Python's `and` / `or` need a single True or False. Use `&` and `|`, and wrap each condition in parentheses.
A slice is a view onto the same memory, not a copy. Writing into it changes the original  use `.copy()` when you need independence.

questions.prompt: For a 2D array `grid`, how do you select column 1 across every row?
questions.explain: The index is `[row, column]`. A bare colon means "all of this dimension".

lessons.title: Shapes that fit together
lessons.lead: Rearranging how values are indexed, and letting NumPy stretch shapes for you.

questions.explain: `-1` means "work this dimension out from the total". 12 elements in 3 rows gives 4 columns.

questions.prompt: Which reshape fixes an "Expected 2D array" error from a flat array?
questions.explain: `reshape(-1, 1)` turns a flat array into a single column, which is the shape scikit-learn and friends expect.

questions.prompt: When are two shapes compatible for broadcasting?
options: Compared from the right, each pair of dimensions is equal or one of them is 1
They have the same number of elements
They have the same number of dimensions
The smaller one divides evenly into the larger one
questions.explain: A `(3,)` row broadcasts across every row of a `(2, 3)` array; a `(2, 1)` column broadcasts across every column.

questions.prompt: Does reshaping change the number of elements in an array?
options: No  the element count must stay the same
Yes, it pads with zeros when needed
questions.explain: reshape only changes how the same values are indexed. A mismatched count raises ValueError.

lessons.title: Vectorised math and axes
lessons.lead: Aggregations collapse an array. The `axis` argument decides in which direction.

questions.prompt: For a 2D array, what does `axis=0` mean in `scores.sum(axis=0)`?
options: Collapse the rows  one result per column
Collapse the columns  one result per row
Sum everything into a single number
questions.explain: Say it out loud: axis=0 collapses rows and gives you a per-column result. axis=1 is the opposite.
axis=1 collapses each row into one number: 80+92+75 and 65+88+91.

options: An array of "pass"/"fail" the same shape as `scores`
The positions where the condition is True
questions.explain: With three arguments, `where` picks element-wise between the two values. With one argument it returns the matching indexes instead.

questions.prompt: Why prefer NumPy operations over a Python loop for numerical work?
options: The loop runs in compiled code across the whole array at once
NumPy automatically uses every CPU core
Python loops cannot do arithmetic on numbers
NumPy arrays use less memory per element than a list, and nothing else changes
questions.explain: Vectorised operations push the loop down into compiled code, which is where the 10–100× speedup comes from. The compact memory layout helps too, but the loop is the point.
